I write about Product Management, Leadership & anything Product Strategy Competitive Advantage Artificial Intelligence Product Management Startup Your Features Aren’t a Moat Anymore Chetan Channa 8 min read · Just now -- Listen Share AI has shortened the time it takes to produce a software feature. If your advantage is that rivals need months to catch up, you don’t have a moat. You have a deadline. The head start is shrinking A lot of what passed for software strategy was implementation lead time: ship first, ship faster, stay ahead of the competition. AI compresses the head start. The obvious objection: Features were never a durable advantage, so nothing has changed. Half right. Reproducing a demo is not the same as shipping secure, reliable, integrated software, and winning a customer is harder than both. But building the first version was a large share of the work, and the time it took was the lead. That lead is what companies used to convert into distribution, contracts and embedded workflows. AI doesn’t remove the harder-to-copy positions; it shortens the window in which a head start can become one. Six sources of advantage, re-scored Only a handful of things make an advantage last . Scale : being cheaper because you’re bigger. Network effects : each new user making the product better for the others. Switching costs : leaving hurts. Brand : customers trusting you enough to choose you, or pay more. Exclusive resources : owning something rivals can’t get. And a business model the incumbent won’t copy, because copying it would hurt them. Below, I take each one and ask: if you’re building an application on a model everyone else can use, and your interface is a chat box, does this still protect you? Fewer do than you’d expect, and the ones that do come with conditions. 1. Scale economies Verdict: earned, not automatic. Traditional software spread big development costs across customers at low incremental cost; the next user was nearly free. AI products add an inference bill to every completed task. Every user makes calls to a model, every call costs money, and more users means more calls. Your cost line now rises with your user line, which software never had to worry about. That inverts a rule every software business was built on: your most engaged user is now your most expensive one . Flat subscriptions assumed the power user was pure upside, and that assumption is what’s breaking. You can watch companies adjust in public: Cursor changed its Pro plan’s frontier-model allowance from request counts to an API-priced usage pool in June 2025. How you pass the cost on to customers is a pricing question, and a separate one. The strategic point: average cost still falls as fixed costs spread, so scale economies don’t vanish, but being big no longer guarantees them. Scale matters when volume produces a persistent cost advantage: better utilisation, purchasing terms, or investments smaller rivals can’t economically match. Reselling frontier-model tokens gives you none of those. Routing routine requests to a small model you run yourself does, if the small model is as good on those requests and the total bill is lower. Owned GPUs alone don’t; idle capacity is a cost, not a barrier. Press enter or click to view image in full size 2. Network effects Verdict: rarely present, often mislabelled. A marketplace has them. A messaging app has them. Most AI products don’t, and “we get smarter with every user” usually describes something else. Three different things hide in that sentence: Per-customer learning. The product learns one customer’s history. Useful, and potentially a switching cost for that customer, but a rival can build the same thing for the next customer, and history that exports easily locks in nobody. Cross-customer learning. One customer’s use improves the product for others. This can be a network effect, if you have the rights to learn across customers, feedback good enough to improve the product, and gains big enough to matter. A participant network. Value rises because participants or counterparties join. Rare in AI products. A support tool that learns from every resolved ticket in one company is case 1. Whether it is case 2 depends on who owns the tickets, 3. whether the vendor may learn across customers, whether the customer can export them, and 4. whether another vendor could reproduce the benefit. Ask those four questions before calling it defensible. Press enter or click to view image in full size 3. A business model the incumbent won’t copy Verdict: the challenger’s best shot, not a lock. AI lets a challenger price per outcome where the incumbent sells seats. That bites only if the incumbent’s seat revenue is large enough that matching would cannibalise it. For eg: Intercom prices its Fin agent per outcome, and Salesforce added per-action Flex Credits alongside seats in 2025. Per action is not per result, and neither proves the economics work. But “won’t copy” has to survive the incumbent trying. Press enter or click to view image in full size 4. Switching costs Verdict: split. Familiarity weakens; integration holds. Switching costs come in two kinds, and AI treats them very differently. The first is familiarity. People spent years learning Photoshop, Excel, Salesforce, SAP, and the learning curve was one of the locks: once you’d put in the hours, starting over somewhere else was expensive.
